description: Search and destroy, Tet, My Lai, Vietnamisation — US and Vietcong tactics and the war's collapse.
content_html:
US Military Strategy: Search and Destroy

General William Westmoreland commanded US forces and adopted a “search and destroy” strategy, using superior firepower and mobility to kill enemy fighters rather than hold territory. US forces used helicopters to insert troops into enemy areas, then withdrew, measuring progress through body counts. The strategy reflected a belief that the USA’s technological advantage would ultimately overwhelm the Vietcong.

The USA also deployed Agent Orange, a chemical defoliant, to strip jungle cover from Vietcong supply routes, and dropped napalm on villages suspected of sheltering enemy fighters. Free-fire zones were designated areas where US troops could shoot at anyone, on the assumption that all residents were hostile. These tactics caused significant civilian casualties.

Key Fact

Operation Rolling Thunder (1965–1968) dropped more bombs on Vietnam than the total dropped in the Second World War. Despite this firepower, the Vietcong continued to recruit and resupply through the Ho Chi Minh Trail, demonstrating the limits of aerial bombardment against a guerrilla enemy.

Vietcong Tactics

North Vietnamese General Vo Nguyen Giap and the Vietcong relied on guerrilla tactics: ambushes, booby traps, hit-and-run raids and a network of underground tunnels at Cu Chi near Saigon. Vietcong fighters were indistinguishable from civilians, making the identification of the enemy extremely difficult for US forces.

The Vietcong also used political terror against village headmen loyal to the South Vietnamese government, and drew on a deep well of nationalist sentiment that resented both the Saigon government and the presence of foreign troops. Giap understood that the USA could not sustain indefinite casualties politically, even if it could militarily: the strategy was to make the war too costly for America to continue.

On 31 January 1968, at the start of the Vietnamese lunar new year (Tet), North Vietnamese and Vietcong forces launched coordinated surprise attacks on more than 100 South Vietnamese towns and cities, including Saigon. The Tet Offensive was militarily repulsed; the attackers suffered massive casualties. But it shattered American public confidence. General Westmoreland had been assuring the public the war was being won; the Tet Offensive proved the enemy was far from defeated. President Johnson’s approval rating collapsed and on 31 March 1968 he announced he would not seek re-election.

On 16 March 1968, US soldiers killed hundreds of unarmed civilians — including women, children and elderly people — in the village of My Lai. The My Lai massacre was covered up initially and not reported publicly until November 1969. When it became known, it intensified domestic and international opposition to the war. It raised fundamental moral questions about the conduct of US forces and the effect of free-fire zone policies on military behaviour.

Vietnamisation and Withdrawal

President Richard Nixon took office in January 1969 and introduced the Vietnamisation policy: gradually withdrawing US troops while training South Vietnamese forces to take over the fighting. US troop numbers fell from 543,000 in 1969 to under 50,000 by 1972. At the same time Nixon secretly bombed and then invaded Cambodia to destroy supply routes.

In May 1970, National Guard troops shot four students dead at Kent State University during an anti-war protest. The killings provoked mass demonstrations across American campuses. In 1971, Daniel Ellsberg leaked the Pentagon Papers to the press, revealing that successive administrations had deliberately misled Congress and the public about the war’s conduct and origins.

Key Fact

The Paris Peace Accords were signed in January 1973, and the last US combat troops left Vietnam in March 1973. US forces had not been defeated on the battlefield, but domestic political pressure, the Tet Offensive’s psychological impact, and the credibility damage of My Lai and the Pentagon Papers made continued involvement untenable.

Opposition to the Vietnam War built steadily from the mid-1960s. College campuses became centres of anti-war activity; draft card burning and sit-ins spread across the country. Television coverage brought the war’s violence directly into American homes in a way no previous conflict had allowed. When Eddie Adams’s photograph of the execution of a Vietcong prisoner on the streets of Saigon was published in February 1968, it became an iconic image of the war’s moral complexity.

The anti-war movement was diverse: it included students, civil rights activists (Martin Luther King Jr. opposed the war from 1967, arguing it diverted resources from domestic poverty), veterans who had served in Vietnam, and mainstream Democrats disillusioned with Johnson’s credibility gap. The movement did not end the war directly, but it constrained the options available to Nixon, who knew that any significant re-escalation would trigger massive domestic unrest. It demonstrated that in a democratic society, public opinion ultimately sets the boundaries of military action.
exam_tip_html: When writing about Vietnam tactics, examiners want both US and Vietcong tactics treated factually and without characterising either side as the ‘aggressor’. Describe Agent Orange, napalm and free-fire zones alongside Vietcong tunnel systems and political terror — the examiner is looking for balance and specific evidence. For questions about US withdrawal, link the military tactics (Vietnamisation) to the domestic political pressure (Tet, My Lai, Kent State, Pentagon Papers) — neither explanation works on its own without the other.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • US tactics — search and destroy, Agent Orange, napalm, free-fire zones — caused significant civilian casualties and failed to defeat a guerrilla enemy who relied on tunnels, ambushes and political support from the population.
  • The Tet Offensive (January 1968) and the My Lai massacre (March 1968, reported 1969) destroyed public confidence in the war effort and contributed directly to LBJ’s decision not to seek re-election.
  • Nixon’s Vietnamisation gradually withdrew US combat troops; the last left in March 1973 following the Paris Peace Accords, but domestic opposition — accelerated by Kent State and the Pentagon Papers — had made continued involvement politically impossible.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the Vietcong used guerrilla tactics against US forces in Vietnam.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct developed ways, each with specific detail (e.g. tunnel systems at Cu Chi; ambushes and booby traps making enemy identification impossible). Secure: Two identified ways with some development. Developing: Two ways identified but not developed. Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the Tet Offensive of 1968 was a turning point in the Vietnam War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed reasons with specific evidence (military failure of the offensive vs its psychological impact; LBJ's decision not to seek re-election; collapse of public confidence). Secure: Two reasons with supporting detail. Developing: Two reasons identified but development limited. Emerging: One basic reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain why opposition to the Vietnam War grew within the United States between 1968 and 1973.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation with multiple causal factors (Tet; My Lai; Kent State; Pentagon Papers; Cambodian invasion) linked coherently to the growth of opposition. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant detail. Developing: Some explanation with limited development. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Nixon's Vietnamisation policy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear features with specific detail (e.g. gradual US troop withdrawal from 543,000 in 1969; training South Vietnamese forces to take over combat). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features without supporting detail. Emerging: One brief feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why US tactics in Vietnam failed to defeat the Vietcong by 1968.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more well-developed causes (guerrilla tactics of the Vietcong; limitations of body count as measure of success; civilian casualties undermining US legitimacy) with causal analysis. Secure: Two causes with relevant evidence. Developing: One cause developed or two briefly stated. Emerging: Simple descriptive statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the My Lai massacre was significant for the Vietnam War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained explanation of its significance (escalation of domestic opposition; moral questions about free-fire zone policies; media reporting; credibility damage to the US government). Secure: Clear explanation with evidence. Developing: Some explanation with limited development. Emerging: Brief descriptive account.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the search and destroy strategy?
flashcard_questions.a: Using US firepower and helicopters to find and kill enemy fighters, measuring success through body counts.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Ho Chi Minh Trail?
flashcard_questions.a: The jungle trail network from North Vietnam through Laos and Cambodia supplying Vietcong forces in the South.
A chemical herbicide used to defoliate jungle cover; its dioxin content caused severe health damage to civilians and veterans.
North Vietnamese military commander who directed Vietcong guerrilla strategy and planned the Tet Offensive.
Coordinated Vietcong surprise attacks on 100+ South Vietnamese cities; militarily repulsed but a major psychological blow to US credibility.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the significance of the Tet Offensive for LBJ?
flashcard_questions.a: His approval collapsed; on 31 March 1968 he announced he would not seek re-election.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the My Lai massacre and when was it reported?
flashcard_questions.a: 16 March 1968; not publicly reported until November 1969.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened at Kent State University, May 1970?
flashcard_questions.a: National Guard troops shot four student anti-war protesters dead, intensifying domestic opposition.
A secret Defense Department history leaked by Daniel Ellsberg in 1971, revealing successive administrations had deceived the public about the war.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the last US combat troops leave Vietnam?
flashcard_questions.a: March 1973, following the Paris Peace Accords signed in January 1973.

glossary_terms.definition: US commander in Vietnam 1964–1968 who pursued the search and destroy strategy, using body counts as a measure of progress.
The count of enemy soldiers killed, used by US commanders as the main measure of progress in Vietnam — widely criticised as misleading.
A chemical herbicide used to defoliate Vietnamese jungle cover; its active ingredient, dioxin, caused severe health damage to civilians and veterans.
A flammable liquid used in bombs and flamethrowers; its use by the US military against villages suspected of sheltering Vietcong became a symbol of civilian harm.
Designated areas in Vietnam where US forces could shoot at any Vietnamese person, on the assumption all residents were hostile.
The network of jungle trails from North Vietnam through Laos and Cambodia used to supply Vietcong forces in the South.
North Vietnamese military commander who directed Vietcong strategy, emphasising guerrilla warfare, patience and the political dimension of the conflict.
The site near Saigon of an extensive Vietcong tunnel system used as headquarters, hospitals and supply lines, stretching over 200 kilometres.
The coordinated surprise offensive launched by North Vietnamese and Vietcong forces on 31 January 1968, attacking over 100 South Vietnamese towns simultaneously.
The killing of unarmed Vietnamese civilians at My Lai village on 16 March 1968 by US soldiers; it intensified domestic opposition when reported in 1969.
US President 1969–1974 who introduced Vietnamisation while secretly expanding the war into Cambodia.
Nixon's strategy of gradually withdrawing US combat troops while training and equipping South Vietnamese forces to take over the fighting.
A neutral country bordering South Vietnam that the USA secretly bombed and then invaded in 1970, triggering widespread anti-war protests.
The American university where National Guard troops shot four student anti-war protesters dead in May 1970.
A former Defense Department analyst who leaked the classified Pentagon Papers to the press in 1971.
A secret Defense Department history of US involvement in Vietnam, leaked in 1971; it revealed that administrations had deceived the public about the war.
